Async cookie allocation, domain bookkeeping, lowest in progress computation and entry execution path are not shown.
Interrupt work handling, completion clearing, tick interaction details and architecture signal backend are not shown.
Exact numeric values and bit positions of flags, shifts, masks, limits and priorities are not shown.
Error handling beyond warnings for duplicate queueing, zero reference per CPU queues and offline targets is not shown.

findings.text: Asynchronous execution offers scheduling by node and domain with device and default domain conveniences, plus waiting for a cookie or for all work in a domain. Scheduling returns a cookie; synchronization blocks until the requested point is reached.
Interrupt-context work offers local queueing and directed queueing to a chosen CPU. Both report whether the item transitioned from idle to pending; an already pending item is left unchanged.
Softirq control offers raising a softirq number while interrupts are already disabled, with a variant that also wakes the per CPU daemon when execution cannot happen on return from interrupt context.

Workqueue control offers adjustment of reserved concurrency for unbound queues and an init-time creation of a dedicated unbound queue for asynchronous work with raised reservation to avoid stalls among interdependent items.

Cross CPU call queueing accepts a single target CPU and a list node, appends it to the remote per CPU queue, and requests an inter processor interrupt only when the queue transitions from empty to non empty.

Queueing distinguishes active work that may run within the concurrency limit from inactive work held behind it. New work joins the inactive backlog whenever such backlog exists, preserving submission order across limit changes.

Unbound pool selection tolerates a race with pool release. A selected queue with zero references causes a retry for unbound queues, while the same condition on a per CPU queue is treated as unexpected.

Concurrency accounting differs by pool kind. Per CPU pools compare the queue active count against the workqueue limit, while unbound pools share a per node counter with a pending list so waiters do not overtake each other.

Async scheduling degrades gracefully under memory shortage or overload. When allocation fails or too much work is outstanding, the caller runs the function synchronously and still consumes a cookie, with the device variant instead reporting inability to defer.
Interrupt work is deduplicated at claim time. An atomic update marks claimed type and observes prior pending state; only the transition into pending proceeds to list insertion and signalling.
Local interrupt work separates lazy items from immediate items into distinct per CPU lists. Lazy items avoid an immediate signal unless tick handling is stopped, while immediate items always signal.
Pool wakeup requires both queued work and absence of running workers, plus availability of an idle worker. Bottom half pools signal through softirq rather than waking a thread.

Unbound CPU choice prefers the requested CPU when allowed, otherwise advances a per CPU round robin cursor over allowed and online CPUs. NUMA placement prefers the local CPU on a matching online node and otherwise defers binding.

Chained execution and async context are detected from the current worker. A worker is considered chained when it runs an item of the queried queue, and async when its current function is the async runner.

Pool state is coordinated under the pool lock. Selection, active slot acquisition, list insertion, idle worker choice and timestamp update all occur while holding it, with wakeup performed after release.

Shared node concurrency uses a node lock only on the slow path. Fast acquisition is lock free; on failure the waiter links into a pending list under the node lock and retries with ordering against release.

Workqueue limit changes serialize under the workqueue mutex. The update publishes new limits, refreshes node limits for unbound queues, then repeatedly activates the first inactive item of each queue while holding each pool lock briefly.

Interrupt work queueing disables preemption around local list insertion and remote queue handoff to stabilize the current CPU view. Softirq raising requires interrupts disabled and may wake the daemon without extra preemption control.
Off queue bookkeeping packs pool identity, disable depth and flags into one word. Helpers extract each field by shifting and masking and repack disable and flags when clearing pending state.

Scheduling state observed includes pool work and idle lists, running count, affinity and priority attributes, per queue active and in flight counters by color, inactive backlog, node active counters with pending lists, and per CPU interrupt work lists.

A work item moves from pending toward either immediate activation or inactive holding, then toward execution when a concurrency slot frees. Freezing can force limits to zero so activation pauses until thaw.

Interrupt work moves from idle to claimed pending to listed, then to signalled unless lazy deferral applies. Remote delivery on some configurations funnels non hard items through a per CPU wakeup item.
Bottom half pool signalling chooses between a remote wakeup item and a local softirq, with priority selecting the softirq flavor. Remote signalling is skipped when already draining on another CPU.
Early initialization creates the async facility on an unbound queue and raises its reserved slots to the default active level, failing loudly if creation is impossible.

Clearing pending before invoking the work function needs strong ordering. Without it a producer store can be missed by a speculative load in the function while the producer also observes pending still set and skips requeue, losing an execution.
Queueing warns on duplicate linkage and on offline targets. A work item already linked is rejected after tracing, and directing interrupt work to an offline CPU is flagged as caller error.

Behavior is parameterized by queue, pool and item flags for unbound, freezable, ordered and bottom half operation, priority selection, lazy and hard interrupt handling, claimed and pending marks, call type discrimination, and sentinel values for unbound CPU and invalid node.
